source.title: Exploring Efficiency Frontiers of Thinking Budget in Medical Reasoning: Scaling Laws between Computational Resources and Reasoning Quality
source.authors: Zi-Qian Bi; Lu Chen; Hong-Ying Luo; Jun-Jie Song; En-Ze Ge; Jun-Min Huang; Tian-Yang Wang; Ke-Yu Chen; C. Liang; Zi-Han Wei; Hua-Feng Liu; Chun-Jie Tian; Jibin Guan; Joe Yeong; Yong-Zhi Xu; Junfeng Hao; Peng Wang

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests downstream scaling by measuring medical-question accuracy against model size, using inference-time thinking budgets rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper measures its own models' accuracy across model sizes and thinking budgets. Its discussion of Kaplan and Hoffmann training-scaling laws is background, not a result from this study. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss or training compute-optimal allocations.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (medical multiple-choice QA with Qwen3 1.7B–235B and DeepSeek-R1 1.5B–70B), the study reports accuracy rising with log model size and fits a log-linear relation. That bears on V6 (downstream predictability with scale). Its main subject, inference-time thinking-budget scaling, matches no version. It does not measure pretraining loss, training compute or allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that medical accuracy follows a log relation in both thinking budget and model size, with diminishing returns past about 256–512 tokens. They name three efficiency regimes (0–256, 256–512, 512+ tokens) and find larger relative gains from thinking for smaller models. Neurology and gastroenterology need deeper reasoning than cardiovascular or respiratory medicine. The authors frame thinking-budget control, not just larger models, as the key lever.
record.recipe_differences: Measures medical multiple-choice accuracy across inference-time thinking budgets and model sizes, rather than held-out pretraining loss across training parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported benefit of thinking budget varies with model size; the paper reports steeper budget-related improvement for smaller models. It also reports differences by medical specialty and task difficulty.

fits_no_version.finding: Medical MCQ accuracy grows logarithmically with inference-time thinking budget (α≈0.08; steeper, α≈0.095, for small models), with diminishing returns beyond about 512 tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time (test-time) compute scaling: downstream accuracy grows roughly log-linearly in reasoning tokens, with diminishing returns.

record.problems: The study measures accuracy on multiple-choice medical datasets, not held-out pretraining loss. It does not explicitly model wall-clock or energy cost, and it notes that DeepSeek-R1's truncation method may interrupt reasoning chains and may not replicate native budget control. Many detailed results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-model and per-dataset curves in Figures 4–16 were not extracted as separate rows because the text does not state their individual numerical values.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute; no loss is measured.
Extrapolation from small runs to large runs.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities or training regimes (repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer).
Relation of downstream accuracy to pretraining loss or training compute. Tasks outside medical MCQ. Out-of-sample prediction of larger models' accuracy.
Dependence of exponents or allocation on fitting and setup choices for training scaling laws.

missing.what: Thinking gain by model size: 15–20% for smaller vs 5–10% for larger models, i.e. the size gap narrows with budget.
Without thinking, Qwen3 generally outperforms DeepSeek-R1 at comparable size, so accuracy is not a function of size alone.
Per-model, per-dataset accuracy curves across model sizes (figures only, no numbers in text).

record.verdict_notes: The Kaplan/Hoffmann formulas in Related Work are background. The proposed L(N,Tb) loss law is not fitted to any loss data. Model sizes are released checkpoints, and the paper does not describe their training, so the size effect is not a controlled scaling experiment. The appendix case tables are single-question anecdotes, not rows.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, training tokens, or training compute.
Whether power-law fits from small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token split under a fixed training-compute budget.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Scaling in other modalities or training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
The study measures medical multiple-choice accuracy against model size, not downstream performance across a broad range of tasks or its relationship to pretraining loss.
Whether fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on setup and fitting choices, or whether training-loss curves bend away from power laws.

rows.subject: Qwen3:235B
rows.note: The paper gives this as an example of larger models outperforming smaller ones.
rows.check: Only one size pair on one dataset, given as an example in Section 4. The thinking budget behind the 62.5% vs 45% is not stated. Released models of different sizes are not controlled scaling runs.

rows.subject: Qwen3 and DeepSeek-R1 (aggregate across tested models and datasets)
rows.size_stated: Qwen3: 1.7B to 235B parameters; DeepSeek-R1: 1.5B to 70B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Fit a reported accuracy relationship with thinking budget and model size
rows.value: Accuracy(Tb, Ms) = α log(Tb + 1) + β log(Ms) + γ + ϵ; α ≈ 0.08, β ≈ 0.12; γ varies by dataset difficulty; ϵ ∼ N(0, σ²), σ ≈ 0.02
rows.note: Reported as an aggregate relationship; the text does not provide the underlying per-model, per-dataset fit results.
rows.check: The fit mixes thinking budget (α term, which fits no version) with model size (β≈0.12, which bears on V6). No per-model residuals, goodness of fit or fitting procedure are reported. Units of β are unclear (accuracy as a fraction vs %). Aggregated across two families that have different no-thinking baselines.

relationships.condition: Medical MCQ accuracy across Qwen3 and DeepSeek-R1 model sizes, 15 datasets
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises with log model size: β≈0.12 with σ≈0.02 (r2), and Qwen3:235B scores 62.5% vs 45% for 1.7B on chief cardiovascular (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased with log model size with β≈0.12 and σ≈0.02, while Qwen3:235B scored 62.5% versus 45% for 1.7B on chief cardiovascular.

relationships.reason: Per the text (no row), thinking gains are 15–20% for smaller vs 5–10% for larger models, so the size advantage shrinks with budget. The scale effect depends on the inference setting.
relationships.display_finding: Extended thinking yielded gains of 15–20% for smaller models versus 5–10% for larger models.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: Medical multiple-choice accuracy across the tested model sizes and datasets
reader_labels.reason: The reported accuracy relationship has a positive model-size coefficient, and Qwen3:235B scores 62.5% versus 45% for Qwen3:1.7B on chief cardiovascular; see r1 and r2.
